title: How to Do Account Research With AI
author: Magnetiz.ai
excerpt: What account research is for, what a brief should include, which sources count, how to check an AI research citation, and how to tell whether the research is right.
content:
Your AI research brief says the account is replacing its finance system. It has a source link. Have you opened the page?

A source link shows where the model says it looked. It does not show what the page said. A model can write a confident sentence, attach a real address, and be wrong about what is on the other side of it. The seller finds out on the call.

This guide covers what account research is for, what a brief should include, which sources count, how to check a citation, and how to tell whether the research is right. The method is the Magnetiz Account Research Playbook, with a worksheet for each step.

Read the playbook →

What is account research?

Account research is finding the public facts about one company that could change what a seller does next. It serves a decision. Should we work this account, what should the first message be about, what do I need before this call, or who else has to be in the deal.

That definition leaves most of a company profile out. Founding year, headquarters and a paragraph of history rarely change a first message. The team the company is hiring for, the work a job post says the new hire will fix, and the tools it names in its own documentation often do.

So good account research starts with the decision and six to eight questions behind it. Each question has to be answerable from a public page, ask for a fact, and have an answer that could change the decision.

Anything only the account can answer is a question for the call. Write those down as well, so the model is never asked to guess them.

Watch for the question "are they a good fit". That is a judgment. A person makes it from the facts.

How do you do account research with AI?

You do account research with AI by having the model propose facts and having something else decide which ones stand. The model reads pages and writes lines. A check with no model in it compares each line's quote with the page it came from.

The playbook runs it in six steps.

  1. Pick the decision and write the questions. One brief serves one decision.
  2. Rank the sources that may be evidence. Primary before secondary, with a list of what is ruled out.
  3. Set what a claim has to carry. One fact to a line, with the page, the exact quote and the date.
  4. Check every citation before a seller reads it. Text compared with text.
  5. Hand over a one-page brief that shows its refusals. What could not be supported is printed.
  6. Read weekly whether the research is right and used. A person opens ten claims and judges them.

The model needs a way to open pages and return their full text. A chat window that answers from memory cannot meet step 3, because there is no fetched page to check a quote against.

Watch for a setup where the model both writes the brief and reviews it. Asking a model to double check its sources returns the same confidence it had the first time.

What sources should account research use?

Account research should prefer primary sources, which are the account saying something about itself. That means its website, careers page, job posts, help center, newsroom and regulatory filings, and a leader's own public posts.

Secondary sources are someone else saying it about the account. News coverage, review sites and data vendor profiles belong here. A claim built on one is still a claim. It is labelled secondary, and a seller treats it as a lead to confirm.

A model cites whatever it finds first, so the ranking has to be written before research starts. Three more decisions belong on the same sheet.

  • What is ruled out. A search snippet for a page that was never opened. A page behind a login the researcher is not entitled to use. The model's own memory of the company.
  • How old is too old. Open roles go stale in days. What the company sells goes stale in months. Each kind of fact gets its own limit.
  • What gets saved. The full text of every page the run opens, with its address and the time. The check needs it.

Watch for the page nearest the account. If a news story quotes the company's announcement, fetch the announcement and cite that.

What should an account research brief include?

An account research brief should include the claims that were supported, each with its exact quote, and the lines that could not be supported, each with the reason. It fits on one page, and a seller never has to click to learn what a page said.

The playbook's template has six sections.

SectionWhat it holdsWho may write it
What the pages sayClaims that passed, each with its quote, page and dateThe model, through the check
What we think it meansReads, each naming the claims it rests onA person, or the model in this section only
What we could not supportRefused lines, each with the reasonThe check
Not foundQuestions no page answered, with the pages triedThe model
Questions for the callWhat only the account can answerYou, once
Check again before actingClaims older than their limitComputed from the fetch dates

Two of those sections do most of the work.

Facts and reads are kept apart. "They are hiring a billing manager" is a fact if a page says so. "They are hiring because the new depot increased invoice volume" is a read unless a page gives that reason. Two true facts joined with "because" go in the second section, with the claim numbers under them.

Refusals stay on the page. A seller who sees what the research could not support does not repeat it on a call. A brief with four claims and three refusals is an honest brief about a thin account.

The CRM Enrichment With Change Review playbook covers the next step, which is deciding what from a brief may be written to the record.

See all six steps in the playbook →

Watch for acting on an old brief. Re-open the page behind a claim before a message goes out about it. A role that was open on Monday can be filled by Friday.

How do you check an AI research citation?

You check an AI research citation by finding the exact quote in the saved text of the page it cites. If the whole quote is there, character for character, the line stands. If it is not, the line is refused.

Four things refuse a line, and each can be decided by a person with the page open or by a short program.

What refuses a lineWhat it catchesHow to see it
No citationA fact the model produced from memoryThe line carries no page and no quote
Quote too shortOne or two words that appear on almost any pageCount the characters, and require 20 or more
Page never fetchedA link the model invented or rememberedLook for the address in the list of pages the run saved
Quote not on the pageA real page credited with words it never saidSearch the saved page text for the whole quote

Two rules keep those four honest. One bad citation refuses the whole line, so a real source cannot cover for an invented one. And nothing is dropped. Claims plus refusals has to equal the number of lines the model proposed.

Here is an invented example. Harborline Logistics moves refrigerated freight, and a seller of invoicing software wants to know what a first message should be about. The run fetches three pages and the model proposes seven lines. The check refuses three.

  • "Harborline uses NetSuite and is replacing it" quoted the job post as saying "lead the move off NetSuite". The page says "lead the move off manual matching". Two words changed, and the claim became the opposite of what the page says.
  • "Harborline has about 450 employees" cited a profile page that was never opened in the run.
  • "It is hiring the billing role because the Tacoma depot increased invoice volume" carried no citation. Both halves were true. No page gave the reason.

The first one is the one to study. It had a working link to a real page about the right role. A reader who checked only that the link worked would have passed it.

Magnetiz runs this check in code in its own research agent, on every brief the agent writes. The check has no model in it. Asked whether a quote is on a page, a model will sometimes say yes when it is close.

Watch for a check that has never refused anything. Feed it a line you made up and confirm it says no.

How do you know your account research is working?

You know account research is working when a person who opens the cited pages agrees with the claims, and sellers report that the claims held up on calls. The citation check cannot tell you either one.

The check proves a page said something on a date. It cannot prove the claim follows from the quote, that the page is right, or that anyone read the brief. So the playbook adds a weekly read in three parts.

  • The numbers the check produces. The share of lines refused, and which refusal. A rise in "no citation" means the model is answering from memory. A share of zero means the check may have stopped running.
  • A sample a person reads. Ten claims that passed, picked at random. Open each page and judge whether the quote supports the claim.
  • What sellers marked. After each call, the seller marks the claims they used as held up, wrong or out of date.

A claim that turned out wrong on a call is the most useful row. Trace it back to its page and its quote, and name what went wrong. The usual causes are a claim that says more than its quote, a reason that was added, a quote about a different company, and a page that was already out of date.

Start with a person reading every brief. Read less only after several weeks with no wrong claim found. Go back to reading everything when the model, the prompt or the page fetcher changes, because the clean record belonged to the old setup.

Watch for judging research by how complete it looks. A long brief with no refusals is more likely to be unchecked than correct.

The pattern across the six steps

Every step moves a decision away from the model that wrote the line. The questions are written by a person. The sources are ranked before the run. The quote is compared by code. The refusals are printed. The sample is read by someone who did not write it.

The playbook has the worksheet for each step, the prompt to paste, and the Harborline account in full with its answer key.

Frequently asked questions

What is account research?

Account research is finding the public facts about one company that could change what a seller does next. It serves one decision, such as what a first message should be about or what to ask on a call. Good account research starts from six to eight questions that a public page could answer, and it leaves judgment to a person.

How do you do account research with AI?

You do account research with AI by having the model open pages and propose one fact to a line, each with the page address, an exact quote and the date. A separate check with no model in it compares every quote with the saved page. Lines that fail are refused and printed in the brief with the reason.

What should an account research brief include?

An account research brief should include the supported claims with their quotes, the reads a person drew from them, the lines that could not be supported, the questions no page answered and the questions to ask on the call. It should fit on one page. Each claim shows its quote, so the seller does not have to click to see what the page said.

How do you check an AI research citation?

You check an AI research citation by searching the saved text of the cited page for the whole quote. The line is refused if it has no citation, if the quote is under about 20 characters, if the page was never fetched in that run, or if the quote is not on the page. One bad citation refuses the whole line.

What sources should account research use?

Account research should use primary sources first. Those are the company's own website, careers page, job posts, help center, newsroom and filings. News coverage, review sites and data vendor profiles are secondary sources, and a claim built on one is labelled so a seller knows to confirm it. Search snippets and the model's memory are ruled out.

Why does AI account research cite pages that say something else?

AI account research cites pages that say something else because the model writes the sentence and the citation together, and nothing compares them afterwards. The link can be real while the claim goes past what the page says. Requiring an exact quote, and checking that quote against the saved page, is what catches it.

How do you know your account research is working?

Account research is working when a person who opens the cited pages agrees with the claims and sellers report that the claims held up on calls. Read three things each week. The share of lines the check refused, ten passed claims opened by a person, and the marks sellers left after their calls.
